# Introduction

> **Do this session if** one function in your model is unknown, it depends on a quantity the model tracks between measurements, and you want to learn its shape while keeping the mechanism you trust.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Coming from R?
UDEs rely on differentiable programming: automatic differentiation through a mechanistic model with a neural network inside it.
R has neural network libraries and R has differential equation solvers, but nothing that differentiates through the two together, which leaves the training loop in this session without a practical R translation.
The Julia ecosystem (SciML, Lux.jl) is currently the most mature platform for this kind of work.
The concepts transfer, and the session is worth reading for them.
:::

## What the course assumes about the second wave

Of the 284 islanders on Tristan da Cunha in 1971, 273 had an attack of influenza and 92 had two, inside 59 days [@mantle1973].
The [SEITL session](seitl.qmd) explains that second wave with a compartment: after recovery you sit in T for a while, and you leave it either back to susceptible or on to lasting immunity.
The [pMCMC session](pmcmc.qmd) then compares two shapes for the time spent in T.

That compartment stands for immunology the 1971 investigation did not measure.
Camacho et al. [-@camacho2011] compared six mechanisms for the same outbreak and found two that the case data support equally well: a window of susceptibility that opens after recovery, and an all-or-nothing response in which some islanders acquire no lasting protection at all.
Their closing recommendation is that separating the two needs immunological data on individuals, which Mantle and Tyrrell's record lacks.

This session takes that recommendation literally.
We replace the compartment with antibody, make protection a function of it, and ask what data would identify that function.

Everything below is simulated.
We generate an outbreak with the island's shape, simulate the surveillance that produced the case record and a serosurvey of the kind that investigation lacked, and fit to those.
The island's real data appear only at the end, where we ask what they could have supported.

## Protection as a function of antibody

Two things protect you after an infection, and they arrive at different times.
The cellular response acts early and fades over a fortnight.
The antibody response builds over days to weeks and then holds, and how high it climbs varies between people: some mount a strong response, others little [@amanna2007; @kucharski2015; @ranjeva2019].

Between the two lies a window in which a person has lost the early protection and has yet to gain the humoral kind.
Islanders whose antibody peaks low stay in that state.
Both of Camacho's surviving mechanisms fall out of the same picture: a delayed climb is the window hypothesis, a low peak is the all-or-nothing one.

The curve that decides both is protection as a function of antibody titre, and its shape is unknown.
Estimates exist for influenza from challenge and field data [@coudeville2010], with 1:40 the conventional half-protective titre, and their uncertainty is wide.

## The model

Infections spread by the renewal equation the earlier sessions use, with generation interval $w$ and reproduction number $R_0$:

$$
\lambda(t) = \frac{R_0}{N} \sum_{s} w_s \, \text{infections}(t - s).
$$

An islander infected $\tau$ days ago has log2 antibody titre

$$
A_c(\tau) = a_c \left(1 - e^{-\tau / r}\right),
$$

where $a_c$ is the peak their response reaches and $r$ is the time the response takes to build.
Their susceptibility to reinfection combines the two kinds of protection:

$$
s_c(\tau) = \left(1 - e^{-(\tau/14)^6}\right)\left(1 - \sigma\left(A_c(\tau)\right)\right).
$$

The first factor climbs from zero as the early protection fades, over about a fortnight.
The second falls towards zero as antibody reaches titres that protect.
An islander is open to reinfection while both factors are near one.

Infections on day $t$ come from the never-infected and from everyone whose susceptibility has returned:

$$
\text{infections}(t) = \lambda(t)\left[S(t) + \sum_{c}\sum_{d < t} n_{c,d}(t)\, s_c(t - d)\right].
$$

Two kinds of data arrive.
Each infection is dated with probability $\rho$, giving Poisson counts, and a serosurvey measures log2 titres with noise of 0.5.

Everything above is supplied except $\sigma$, the protection curve, which this session learns.

## Why this needs a UDE

A **universal differential equation** (UDE) keeps the mechanism and replaces an unknown term with a neural network [@rackauckas2020].
Here the network supplies $\sigma$, constrained to increase with titre and to stay between zero and one, which is everything we are willing to assert about it.

The input to $\sigma$ is the titre an islander has on the day they are exposed, which the model computes from their infection date and the antibody curve.
A serosurvey measures titres on the days blood is drawn, and the exposures happen on all the other days.
Because the titre at exposure depends on the antibody parameters, and the infections depend on $\sigma$ evaluated at that titre, the function and the epidemic have to be fitted together.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Which data identify which part

The protection curve enters the model through a composition: the case data see susceptibility as a function of time since infection, which is $\sigma$ evaluated along the antibody curve.
Cases alone therefore constrain the composition rather than either piece.
Much of this session is about which data break that apart, and the answer decides what a study would have to collect.
:::

# Objectives

By the end of this session, you will be able to:

1. Replace an assumed compartment with a mechanism whose unknown part is a function of a measurable quantity
2. Fit a neural network inside that mechanism to two data streams at once
3. Recognise a likelihood that is flat in the direction you care about, and say what it means
4. Show that a second data stream identifies the mechanism, and that the timing of its collection decides whether it does
5. Work out which measurements identify the mechanism, and check the island's record against them

## The simulated outbreak

We simulate the island's epidemic with a protection curve that rises in two steps, and then set that curve aside until the end.

```{julia}
run = outbreak(ANTIBODY_RISE, true_protection)
cases = report_cases(run.infections)
days = 0:TDC_DAYS

println("infections ", round(Int, sum(run.infections)), ", of which second infections ",
    round(Int, sum(run.second)))
println("simulated dated cases ", sum(cases),
    " (the island's record has 312, from 365 attacks, 92 of them second)")
println("first peak ", maximum(cases[1:20]), " on day ", argmax(cases[1:20]),
    "; second wave peaks at ", maximum(cases[26:end]), " on day ", argmax(cases[26:end]) + 25)
```

```{julia}
plot(days, cases, linewidth = 2, label = "dated cases", xlabel = "Day",
    ylabel = "Cases", title = "A simulated outbreak on an island")
plot!(days, TDC_REPORTING .* run.second, linewidth = 2, label = "second infections")
```

The second wave is made of people who have already had influenza once.
In this simulated island they are the weak responders, whose antibody peaks below any protective level, together with the intermediate ones, who reach the shoulder of the protection curve and are slowed rather than stopped.
The two groups are 38% of the population between them.

## The simulated serosurvey

We simulate eighty islanders giving blood twice, on day 20 and at the end of the outbreak.
Their infection dates come from the case record, so each sample gives a titre at a known time since infection.

```{julia}
sera = draw_sera(run.infected, ANTIBODY_RISE)
tau = [sample[3] - sample[2] for sample in sera]
titres = [sample[4] for sample in sera]

scatter(tau, titres, markersize = 3, alpha = 0.6, label = "",
    xlabel = "Days since infection", ylabel = "log2 titre",
    title = "Simulated titres by time since infection")
```

The first bleed catches people while their antibody is still climbing, and the second finds them at their peak.
The samples settle at three levels, which are the three kinds of responder: most islanders reach a protective titre, some an intermediate one, and a fifth stay low.

# Learning the protection curve

The network takes a log2 titre and returns protection between zero and one.

```{julia}
#| output: false

network = protection_network()
p_init, network_state = protection_weights(network)

curve(p) = protection_from(p, network, network_state) ## the learned protection curve

## the case series alone, at the antibody rise time we assume
cases_only(p, rise) = -case_loglik(outbreak(rise, curve(p)).infections, cases)

## the case series and the serosurvey together
with_sera(p, rise) = cases_only(p, rise) - sero_loglik(sera, rise)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## What you know goes into the network too

The case series sees a second wave and cannot see who is in it.
A curve that *falls* as titre rises explains that wave just as well, by casting the strong responders as the susceptible group and the weak ones as protected, and on this case series it comes within four log likelihood units of the truth.
Gradient descent from an unlucky start settles there and reports it without any sign of trouble.

Protection rises with antibody, and that is knowledge, so it belongs in the architecture.
`monotone` takes the absolute value of every weight, which makes the network increasing in its input and removes the mirror solution from the space the optimiser searches.
`fit_protection` then trains from three sets of starting weights and keeps the best, which guards against the ordinary kind of local optimum.
:::

```{julia}
p_cases, _, history = fit_protection(p -> cases_only(p, ANTIBODY_RISE), network)
println("network parameters: ", length(p_init))
println("loss on the case series: ", round(cases_only(p_cases, ANTIBODY_RISE), digits = 1))
for titre in (3.0, 5.0, 7.0)
    println("  protection at log2 titre ", titre, ": learned ",
        round(network_protection(titre, p_cases, network, network_state), digits = 2),
        ", true ", round(true_protection(titre), digits = 2))
end
```

```{julia}
fitted = TDC_REPORTING .* outbreak(ANTIBODY_RISE, curve(p_cases)).infections

scatter(days, cases, markersize = 3, color = :black, label = "simulated cases",
    xlabel = "Day", ylabel = "Cases", title = "The fitted epidemic")
plot!(days, fitted, linewidth = 2, label = "fitted")
```

The fit reproduces both waves, which is the least it should do: the protection curve has 25 parameters and the epidemic is one curve of 60 numbers.
A fit this good tells you the model can describe the outbreak, but it leaves the mechanism inside it untested.

```{julia}
titre_grid = range(0, 9, length = 200)
learned(p) = [network_protection(t, p, network, network_state) for t in titre_grid]

plot(titre_grid, true_protection.(titre_grid), linewidth = 3, color = :black,
    label = "True protection", xlabel = "log2 titre", ylabel = "Protection",
    title = "Protection fitted with the rise time assumed correct")
plot!(titre_grid, learned(p_cases), linewidth = 2, label = "Learned")
```

Given the right antibody curve, the case series puts the curve in the right place: protection passes one half at a log2 titre of about five, where the truth does, and the two agree at the top and bottom of the range.
The two steps in the truth are smoothed into one, which is the first sign of where the information runs out.
That fit was handed the antibody rise time, and the next section asks what happens when a study has to estimate it.

# One epidemic, many protection curves

The antibody rise time was handed to the fit.
Change it and the network compensates, because the cases only ever see the product of the two.
The profile below refits the network at each assumed rise time, with the case series alone and with the sera added.

```{julia}
profile = CSV.read(datadir("tdc_protection_profile.csv"), DataFrame)
losses = unique(profile[:, [:rise, :data, :loss]])
unstack(losses, :rise, :data, :loss)
```

```{julia}
plot(xlabel = "Assumed antibody rise time (days)", ylabel = "Loss",
    title = "Each dataset's loss against the assumed rise time")
for (label, marker) in (("cases", :circle), ("final sera", :diamond), ("serial sera", :square))
    rows = sort(losses[losses.data .== label, :], :rise)
    plot!(rows.rise, rows.loss, linewidth = 2, marker = marker, label = label)
end
vline!([ANTIBODY_RISE], linestyle = :dash, color = :grey, label = "truth")
```

The case series barely moves: three quarters of a log likelihood unit separates its best and worst rise times across the whole range from three to eleven days.
Its minimum sits at eight, ahead of the truth at six by two hundredths of a unit, which is nothing at all.
The network absorbs a wrong antibody curve and reproduces the same epidemic through it.
The serial sera, by contrast, move by 254 units over the same range and put their minimum on six.

```{julia}
#| output: false

function weights_for(rise, label)
    rows = sort(profile[(profile.rise .== rise) .& (profile.data .== label), :], :index)
    p = copy(p_init)
    p .= rows.value
    return p
end
```

```{julia}
plot(titre_grid, true_protection.(titre_grid), linewidth = 3, color = :black,
    label = "True protection", xlabel = "log2 titre", ylabel = "Protection",
    title = "Five fits to the same case series")
for rise in unique(profile.rise)
    plot!(titre_grid, learned(weights_for(rise, "cases")), linewidth = 1.5,
        linestyle = :dash, label = "rise = $rise days")
end
plot!()
```

Every curve in that figure fits the epidemic.
They disagree about where protection arrives: the titre at which it reaches one half moves from about four, under an assumed rise time of eleven days, to about seven, under three days.
The longer the antibody is assumed to take to build, the lower the titre at which the fitted curve places protection, because the epidemic only ever sees the two multiplied together.
Three doublings of titre separate the ends, and one doubling is the difference between a titre that protects an islander and one that leaves them open to a second attack.

::: {.callout-important}
## Extra flexibility is spent on the wrong thing

The case data identify susceptibility as a function of time since infection.
Splitting that into an antibody curve and a protection curve needs a second kind of measurement.
A more flexible network makes this worse rather than better: the extra freedom is spent absorbing the wrong antibody curve, and the fit improves while the answer drifts.
:::

# What a serosurvey adds

The sera speak about the antibody curve, which is the part the cases leave open.
Let each dataset pick its own rise time, and compare the protection curves that follow.

```{julia}
chosen = Dict{String, Float64}()
for label in unique(losses.data)
    rows = losses[losses.data .== label, :]
    chosen[label] = rows.rise[argmin(rows.loss)]
    println(rpad(label, 14), "picks a rise time of ", chosen[label], " days (truth ",
        ANTIBODY_RISE, ")")
end
```

```{julia}
plot(titre_grid, true_protection.(titre_grid), linewidth = 3, color = :black,
    label = "True protection", xlabel = "log2 titre", ylabel = "Protection",
    title = "Protection curves from the three datasets")
for (label, style) in (("cases", :solid), ("final sera", :dash), ("serial sera", :solid))
    rise = chosen[label]
    plot!(titre_grid, learned(weights_for(rise, label)), linewidth = 2,
        linestyle = style, label = "$label, rise = $rise days")
end
plot!()
```

```{julia}
for label in ("cases", "final sera", "serial sera")
    p = weights_for(chosen[label], label)
    values = [round(network_protection(t, p, network, network_state), digits = 2)
              for t in (3.0, 5.0, 7.0)]
    println(rpad(label, 14), "protection at log2 titre 3/5/7: ", values)
end
println(rpad("truth", 14), "protection at log2 titre 3/5/7: ",
    [round(true_protection(t), digits = 2) for t in (3.0, 5.0, 7.0)])
```

The serial sera pick six days and recover the curve.
The case series picks eight days and the final survey eleven, and both slide protection down to titres where it has not arrived: at a log2 titre of 5 they report 0.75 and 0.91 against a true 0.51.
An analyst working from either would call an islander at that titre safe when they were about as likely as not to be reinfected, and would report an island better protected than it was.

The identification comes from the first bleed, on day 20, when antibody is still climbing and its rate leaves a trace.
By the end of the outbreak everyone has reached their peak, and a titre at the plateau says how high the response climbed rather than how fast.

## How much of that curve is pinned down

A single fit gives a single curve.
To see how much the noise in the data moves it, the script refits eight times to resampled case counts and a resampled serosurvey, holding the rise time at the value the serial sera chose.
Each refit restarts three times, so the spread below is uncertainty rather than the optimiser giving up in different places.

```{julia}
ensemble = CSV.read(datadir("tdc_protection_ensemble.csv"), DataFrame)
members = [begin
               rows = sort(ensemble[ensemble.replicate .== r, :], :index)
               p = copy(p_init)
               p .= rows.value
               p
           end for r in unique(ensemble.replicate)]

plot(titre_grid, true_protection.(titre_grid), linewidth = 3, color = :black,
    label = "True protection", xlabel = "log2 titre", ylabel = "Protection",
    title = "Eight fits to resampled data")
for (i, p) in enumerate(members)
    plot!(titre_grid, learned(p), linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.7, color = 2,
        label = i == 1 ? "resampled fits" : "")
end
plot!(titre_grid, learned(weights_for(chosen["serial sera"], "serial sera")),
    linewidth = 2.5, color = 1, label = "fit to the simulated data")
```

```{julia}
predictions = [TDC_REPORTING .* outbreak(ANTIBODY_RISE, curve(p)).infections
               for p in members]
lower = [minimum(pred[i] for pred in predictions) for i in eachindex(days)]
upper = [maximum(pred[i] for pred in predictions) for i in eachindex(days)]

plot(days, lower, fillrange = upper, fillalpha = 0.3, linealpha = 0, color = 1,
    label = "range across the eight fits", xlabel = "Day", ylabel = "Cases",
    title = "Epidemics the fitted curves produce")
plot!(days, predictions[1], linewidth = 2, color = 1, label = "one of them")
scatter!(days, cases, markersize = 3, color = :black, label = "simulated cases")
```

The eight curves agree at the bottom and top of the titre range and disagree across the middle, which is exactly where the true curve has its shoulder.
That middle stretch is the part the data speak least about, and it is the part that distinguishes a curve with two steps from a plain logistic.

The epidemics those curves produce sit on the data throughout.
The band has no width during the first wave, because protection plays no part in infecting islanders who have never been infected, and it opens up in the second wave, where the curves disagree.
Models that differ about immunology can agree about the epidemic.

This ensemble is a rough sampling distribution rather than a posterior.
It moves the data and refits, so it shows how much the noise moves the answer, and it holds the rise time fixed, so it leaves out the uncertainty that the profile above makes visible.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: when to draw blood"}
The two serosurveys cost the same and differ only in timing.
Say why the day 20 bleed pins down the rise time and the final one leaves it open, in terms of the antibody curve, and work out roughly when you would draw blood in an outbreak where the response took a month to build.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="What to look for" collapse="true"}
The rise time appears in the antibody curve as $a_c(1 - e^{-\tau/r})$, and the data can only see it while the exponential term is still moving.
By day 59 most of the sampled islanders are 40 to 55 days past infection, where $e^{-\tau/r}$ is tiny for any rise time between 3 and 11 days, so every candidate predicts the same titre.
The day 20 bleed finds people 10 to 20 days past infection, where the candidates predict titres that differ by more than the assay noise.

For a response that takes a month to build, the informative window moves accordingly: bleeds in the first four to six weeks after infection separate the candidates, and a survey at three months finds everyone at their plateau again.
The general rule is that a measurement informs a rate only while the quantity it measures is changing at that rate.
:::

# What the learned curve says about the island

```{julia}
p_best = weights_for(chosen["serial sera"], "serial sera")
labels = ("strong", "intermediate", "weak")
sus(class, p) = [(1 - early_protection(t)) *
                 (1 - network_protection(antibody_level(class, t, ANTIBODY_RISE), p,
                                         network, network_state)) for t in 0:TDC_DAYS]

true_sus(class) = [(1 - early_protection(t)) *
                   (1 - true_protection(antibody_level(class, t, ANTIBODY_RISE)))
                   for t in 0:TDC_DAYS]

for (c, label) in enumerate(labels)
    learned_s, true_s = sus(c, p_best), true_sus(c)
    println(rpad(label, 14), "peak susceptibility ", round(maximum(learned_s), digits = 2),
        " on day ", argmax(learned_s) - 1, ", settling at ", round(learned_s[end], digits = 2),
        " (truth ", round(maximum(true_s), digits = 2), " on day ", argmax(true_s) - 1,
        ", settling at ", round(true_s[end], digits = 2), ")")
end

plt = plot(layout = (1, 2), size = (900, 400), bottom_margin = 5Plots.mm,
    left_margin = 3Plots.mm)
for (c, label) in enumerate(labels)
    plot!(plt[1], 0:TDC_DAYS, [antibody_level(c, t, ANTIBODY_RISE) for t in 0:TDC_DAYS],
        linewidth = 2, label = label, xlabel = "Days since infection",
        ylabel = "log2 titre", title = "Antibody", titlefontsize = 10)
    plot!(plt[2], 0:TDC_DAYS, sus(c, p_best), linewidth = 2, color = c, label = label,
        xlabel = "Days since infection", ylabel = "Susceptibility",
        title = "Susceptibility: learned (solid) and true (dashed)", titlefontsize = 10)
    plot!(plt[2], 0:TDC_DAYS, true_sus(c), linewidth = 2, color = c, linestyle = :dash,
        label = "")
end
plt
```

The learned curve, applied along the three antibody trajectories, reproduces the mechanism behind the island's second wave.
A strong responder opens to 0.03 on day 13, against a true 0.04 on the same day: the early protection has faded and the titre is nearly at its peak, so the window exists and is narrow.
An intermediate responder reaches 0.68 and settles at 0.61, where the truth is 0.52 and 0.51, so a second attack is slowed and the fit overstates by about a fifth.
A weak responder returns to full susceptibility and stays there, which is a fifth of the island.

Both of Camacho's surviving hypotheses appear here as features of one curve.
The brief dip in the strong responders is their window of susceptibility.
The flat high susceptibility of the weak responders is their all-or-nothing response.
A study with serial sera would tell you how much of each the island had, which the case series alone cannot.

# What a study would have to collect

::: {.callout-warning}
## The island's record holds 11 sera against this session's 160

Mantle and Tyrrell recovered sera from 11 islanders, at one time point [@camacho2011].
Everything above rests on 160 samples from 80 people bled twice, with infection dates attached.
The session shows what such a study would buy, which is a different claim from having measured it.

The design question is the transferable part.
Before collecting immunological data to settle a mechanism, work out which parameter the mechanism turns on, then check that your sampling times fall where that parameter still moves the measurement.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise: the analysis you could run on the real data"}
The real record gives dated attacks, the counts of first and second attacks, and 11 cross-sectional sera.
Which parts of this session's model could you fit to that, and which would you have to fix by assumption?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="What to look for" collapse="true"}
The case series and the 92 second attacks constrain susceptibility as a function of time since infection, which a compartment model such as SEITL can absorb, and the course already fits that.
The 11 sera give the titre distribution at one moment, which bears on the spread of peaks across people rather than on the rate of climb.

The protection curve stays out of reach: it needs titres at known times since infection, and the record has neither the times nor enough people.
Fixing the antibody curve by assumption would make the protection curve estimable, and the profile in this session shows what that estimate would be worth, since a wrong assumption about the rise time moves the curve from one end of the titre range to the other.
:::

# When to use UDEs

## UDEs are a good fit when

- You trust the mechanism and can name the one function you do not know
- That function depends on a quantity the model tracks between measurements
- The question needs the mechanism: a new population, a scenario, or an intervention
- The data cover the range of the input the question will use

## Other methods are a better fit when

- The unknown function's input is measured at the times it is used. A parametric form or a spline in that covariate, fitted with MCMC, is simpler and gives uncertainty
- A form with a few interpretable parameters fits adequately, in which case prefer it
- The likelihood is flat in the direction you care about. Extra flexibility widens the flat direction, and the fix is data of another kind

# Comparison with other approaches

| Method | What it learns | Identifies the mechanism | Uncertainty | Data needs | Cost |
|--------|----------------|--------------------------|-------------|------------|------|
| **Compartment with an assumed shape** | A duration | No | Easy with MCMC | Case series | Low |
| **Parametric protection curve** | Two or three parameters | Given sera at known times | Easy with MCMC | Cases and sera | Low |
| **UDE with a state-dependent term** | The shape of the curve | Given sera at known times | Hard | Cases and sera | High |

# Where UDEs have been applied

Real-data applications are still relatively few.
In epidemiology, Kuwahara and Bauch [-@kuwahara2024] used a UDE informed by behaviour and mobility data to predict COVID-19 waves, Schmid et al. [-@schmid2026] combined a UDE-based SEIR model with wastewater surveillance to project case counts, and Rojas-Campos et al. [-@rojas2023] demonstrated the UDE-to-SINDy pipeline on simulated regional transmission data.
Philipps et al. [-@philipps2025] review the state of UDEs in systems biology and note that most published work still uses synthetic data.

# Learning points

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning points"}
- **A compartment can hide a mechanism**: replacing T with antibody turns a duration you assume into a curve you can estimate, and makes the assumption visible
- **UDEs learn a function of something the model tracks**: here the titre at exposure, which the sera measure on other days
- **What you know goes into the network**: protection rises with antibody, and a network free to learn otherwise finds a mirror solution that the case series rejects by only four log likelihood units
- **A flat likelihood is a result**: the case series constrains susceptibility against time since infection, and splitting that into an antibody curve and a protection curve needs data of another kind
- **Timing decides whether a measurement identifies a rate**: bleeds on day 20 pin the antibody rise, and the same islanders bled at the end say as little as the cases do
- **Competing mechanisms can be one curve**: a window of susceptibility and an all-or-nothing response are the strong and weak ends of the same protection curve
- **Simulating the study is the cheap part of designing it**: the profile here costs minutes and would have told Mantle and Tyrrell when to take blood
:::

# Going further

## From a learned curve to an equation

Once the curve has a shape, look for a formula.
**Symbolic regression** searches for an equation that reproduces it, either by sparse regression over candidate terms, as in SINDy [@brunton2016], or by evolving expressions [@cranmer2020symbolic].
Our learned protection curve is a logistic in the log2 titre, which is the form the serology literature already uses [@coudeville2010], with two parameters to estimate.
Refitting that way brings the problem back to MCMC and gives credible intervals on the curve and on everything computed from it.

## The parts we supplied

The reproduction number, the reporting probability, the generation interval, the peaks of the two kinds of response and their proportions were all handed to the fit.
A real analysis estimates them, and each one competes with the protection curve for the same information.
The profile in this session is the two-parameter version of that problem, and the full version is a joint posterior over every supplied quantity and the network weights together.

## Beyond antibody

The same structure fits any mechanism where protection or infectiousness depends on a measured quantity: viral load and onward transmission, cellular markers and severity, or antibody and vaccine response.
The question to ask in each case is which of your measurements are taken while the quantity is changing.

# Next session

This session and the [variational inference](variational_inference.qmd) session round out the course's coverage of inference methods.
Together with the MCMC, particle filter and pMCMC sessions, you now have a range of approaches for fitting mechanistic models to data, and some sense of when each is appropriate.
